headline: Klondike Wreck 8-19, 210 Feet: Bluefin Slots Stacked, Sea Bass to 4 Pounds Inshore
subhead: The tuna are holding tighter to the beach than they should this deep into July, and the reef sites are still paying the bills while boats wait for a weather window to the canyons.
body_markdown:
Two-hundred-ten feet. That's what the sounder read Tuesday morning sitting over Klondike wreck 8-19, and the bait column stacked from 140 down to the deck was thick enough that I made three passes before I even dropped a jig. Twenty years of running this piece of water and I've learned that when the bait's holding that deep in July, it's because the thermocline's doing something interesting — and sure enough, we found a clean break at 68 feet, cooler water underneath pushing that bait tight and giving the bluefin a reason to sit on the structure instead of running the open lumps.

We flagged this last week — said the warm-water filaments pushing toward the Hudson and Wilmington canyon approaches would put yellowfin and mahi within range of the Jersey fleet, and that's exactly the window that's cracking open right now. Buoy 44025 out in the Bight is reading 71.2 degrees on the surface, which doesn't sound like much until you factor in the blue water pushing inshore on those eddies. That's canyon color showing up closer to the beach than it has any business being in mid-July, and it's why guys running out of Manasquan and Belmar are covering the Wilmington approach in a day trip instead of an overnighter.

The bluefin bite itself has been steady rather than spectacular, which is fine by me — steady is what pays for fuel. We're inside the slot window now, 27 inches to just under 47, two-fish limit, and the fish cooperating on that class have been sitting on the Mud Hole lumps in 120 to 160 feet, particularly the hump just east of the Chicken Canyon drop where the bottom breaks sharp. Green machines and small cedar plugs behind the spreader bars have been drawing strikes on the troll around daybreak, and once the sun gets up we've had better luck slowing the spread down and working ballyhoo naked baits through the same water. Nobody's boating giants right now — the trophy category's been closed since July 3rd — but a 34-inch bluefin on 30-pound tackle still makes for a good morning, and we've had multiple-fish mornings three trips out of the last five. That's a solid number for this time of year, though it's not automatic — you need to be on the temperature break at first light, not chasing it at nine.

Mahi are starting to mix in around anything floating out past the Mud Hole edge — lobster pot warps, weed clumps, the odd pallet. Nothing dramatic yet, a fish or two per stop, but that's how the August pattern usually starts. If you're running past a pot with any color of weed hanging off the buoy line, it's worth a pitch bait or a small feather before you keep moving. I expect that pattern to build through the next two to three weeks as the water keeps warming.

Inshore, the reef and wreck network is carrying the week for anyone who doesn't want to burn the fuel to run offshore in that leftover swell — 44025 was showing close to four feet at five seconds Tuesday, short and choppy, uncomfortable enough that I kept my six-pack trip tucked in tighter to the beach than planned. Sea Girt Reef in 60 to 70 feet has been holding good numbers of black sea bass, fish running 14 to 17 inches with a scattering of 4-pounders mixed in on the deeper pieces. Same story at Axel Carlson Reef, a little shallower at 55 feet, and Shrewsbury Rocks has been quietly productive too if you can find the right piece of structure among the boulders — that's not a spot you fish blind, you need a number in the book or a very patient sounder pass. Green crab and squid strips on a double-hook bottom rig, 3/0 hooks, 4 to 6 ounces of lead depending on drift speed, has been the standard producer. Jigging bucktails tipped with Gulp works too when the current's moving hard enough to keep them off bottom, and it thins out the throwbacks faster than bait soak.

Barnegat Ridge has been a mixed bag — some boats scoring well on sea bass in the 80-foot depths off the northern end, others reporting a slower pick. My read is the fish are there but scattered across a wider stretch of structure than usual, which means covering ground on the drift rather than anchoring up on one number pays off right now.

Tog season's closed this time of year so I'm not chasing blackfish, and cod are strictly a cold-water target we won't see again until late fall. Bonito haven't shown in our water yet — the temperature signature isn't quite there — but with water pushing into the high 60s and low 70s up toward Montauk and the Vineyard, I'd start watching the temperature breaks off Sea Girt and Shrewsbury by early August.

Looking ahead, if the high pressure holds like it's been holding, I'd put my next trip on the Mud Hole lumps at first light for bluefin, then work back inshore to Sea Girt or Axel Carlson for a sea bass bag once the sun's up and the tuna bite typically slows. That's the play as long as the wind stays cooperative — if it swings onshore and builds that swell back up, I'd scrap the offshore leg entirely and just fish structure close to the inlet.
